newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says U.S. shouldn't expect grain export cap.
newsitem.headline: Canada says U.S. shouldn't expect grain export cap.

text.p: The United States should not expect any movement from Canada to restrict its grain exports when officials from the two countries meet in Ottawa next week, a spokesman for Canadian Trade Minister Sergio Marchi said on Wednesday.
"They should not come up here with expectations of negotiating a curb or cap on Canadian grain exports," spokesman Charles Larabie said in a phone interview. "That is not going to happen."
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Wednesday that U.S. and Canadian officials will meet in Ottawa on June 27 for new discussions about the grain trade.

Farmers in the northern U.S. plains have complained for years of unfair imports of Canadian wheat. The Clinton administration has told Canada it would take action if the shipments exceeded 1.5 million tonnes a year.
In Ottawa, Larabie said there is a possibility that grain shipments would top that amount but he would not know for about another month.
In 1995, Canada agreed to cap exports at 1.5 million tonnes for the year.
Barshefsky has also been under pressure to seek removal of Canadian tariffs on U.S. dairy products.
But Larabie said Canada was not willing to budge in that area either.

"We're not in a trade negotiation here," he said. "We will not be entertaining any kind of trade negotiations on agriculture until at the earliest 1999 when the agenda for the WTO (World Trade Organization) kicks back in."
Complaints about Canada's potato exports are also off the mark, Larabie said.
"That's a market we're getting access to fair and square because there's a market demand for Canadian potatoes," he said.
Barshefsky said the U.S. International Trade Commission was reviewing the potato trade between Canada and the United States following complaints of unfairly low-priced Canadian exports.
The United States challenged Canada's controls on dairy, poultry and livestock imports but lost the case before a North American Free Trade Agreement panel.

"If the Americans don't like the result, well, that's unfortunate for them but we have to move on to other things," Larabie said. "We are not going to revisit every issue in which the U.S. loses a panel."
